catalog_quote: Na língua Yuhup os morfemas são predominantemente monossilábicos, exceto nos casos de reduplicação. Seu sistema acentuai é previsível e obedece aos seguintes critérios: 3.1. Regras Acentuais em Yuhup • O acento primário recai na última sílaba da palavra e o secundário na primeira. • Os sufixos marcados com extramétricos nunca são acentuados, com exceção do sufixo de plural. • Nas palavras que possuem dois sufixos, ambos são extramétricos. ... 3.2. Inventário das Regras Acentuais Com base na teoria de Halle & Vergnaud (1987), da Fonologia Métrica, apresentaremos as regras que definirão o padrão acentua! da língua Yuhup. sweep_summary: One item in the sweep: Walker 2002 (NELS 32), already listed in the per-language bibliography. Previous audit could not obtain it (scholarworks 403; the USC asset URL cited by Semantic Scholar is dead). Located the author's copy on Rachel Walker's UCSC site (publications page) and fetched sources it with wget (curl was refused by the CampusPress host); (+.txt),. The paper is about augmentation in the locative/future suffixes; its only stress statement (p. 552) is background taken from Lopes & Parker 1999: 332: main stress on the last stem syllable, suffixes generally excluded from the stem domain, stressed vowels lengthen, every morpheme contributing exactly one syllable. This CONFIRMS the catalog's MORPHOLOGICAL coding based on Lopes 1995 (stem-final primary stress, suffixes extrametrical) and does not supersede it (second-hand; silent on the plural-suffix exception and secondary stress). Not in the item list but flagged from Walker's citations: Lopes & Parker 1999, 'Aspects of Yuhup Phonology', IJAL 65(3): 324-342 (doi 10.1086/466393, paywalled per the earlier audit), p. 332 is the pinpointed published first-hand stress statement and would be the best acquisition target (high priority) if a copy becomes available. all look-ups were done through APIs (Semantic Scholar, Glottolog) and direct fetches.

Suffixes are generally excluded (see (4b)) — they appear to stand outside of the stem domain (L&P 1999: 332). (4) a. [ˈtæ̃ːh] 'son' [miâh-ˈnãːw̃] 'paca rodent' b. new_statements.reading: Main stress is on the last syllable of the stem; suffixes are (generally) outside the stress domain, so stress is stem-final regardless of suffixation; the stressed vowel lengthens. This is a second-hand statement (explicitly drawn from Lopes & Parker 1999: 332, the published IJAL version of the catalog's source Lopes 1995), so it is an independent published restatement rather than new first-hand data. It confirms the catalog's MORPHOLOGICAL coding (stress fixed at the right edge of the stem domain, ordinary suffixes extrametrical) and is silent on the plural-suffix exception and on secondary stress.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the RO1-R06 metrical rules are verbatim in the held Lopes 1995 PDF at the stated place (printed pp. 57-60 = PDF pp. 65-67; conclusion p. 120), scanned noise aside. (2) Deciding source is a 137-pp 1995 MA phonology thesis (UFSC, co-supervised by Parker) with a dedicated stress chapter; the held Silva & Silva 2012 grammar sketch (pp. 80-81) independently states accent is predictable, always on the last syllable, coinciding with contour tones on the last syllable of roots — consistent with our stem-final/morphological coding. (3) Two better-credentialed works are not held: the IJAL 1999 revision (paywalled, doi 10.1086/466393) and Ospina Bozzi's 484-pp 2002 Paris-7 grammar of Colombian Yuhup (print only; theses.fr record fetched sources). sources.note: The paper is about the prosodic morphology of the locative (-CVt) and future (-CVp) suffixes (augmentation analysis in OT); stress is mentioned only as background, and explicitly on the authority of Lopes & Parker 1999 (IJAL 65: 324-342; the author thanks Parker and Lopes for help). Statement: main stress falls on the last STEM syllable; suffixes are 'generally excluded' from the stress domain (stand outside the stem domain, L&P 1999: 332); stressed vowels lengthen. Also: every morpheme contributes exactly one syllable to a word (L&P 1999: 325), so stems are mostly monosyllabic. No mention of…
